Q178275.title: 1918 influenza pandemic ('Spanish flu')
paras: The influenza pandemic of 1918 to 1920 was one of the deadliest in history. It was caused by an H1N1 strain of influenza A, infected an estimated 500 million people, nearly a third of the world's population, and killed somewhere between 17 million and 50 million, possibly as many as 100 million.

Its origin is uncertain. The earliest probable cases were recorded in Kansas in the United States in early 1918, with cases in France, Germany and Britain in April, though some researchers argue that the virus had arisen years earlier. It came to be called the 'Spanish flu' only because Spain, neutral in the First World War and free of wartime censorship, reported on it openly from late May 1918, while the warring countries suppressed news of it to protect morale.

The pandemic came in waves. The first, in the spring of 1918, was mostly mild. A second, far deadlier wave spread in the autumn of 1918, carried by troops moving in crowded ships and trains at the end of the war: victims could die within hours or days, their lungs filling with fluid. Unusually, many of the dead were healthy young adults; more American soldiers died of the flu than in battle. With no vaccine or antiviral drugs, authorities closed schools, churches and theatres, ordered masks and banned spitting. Cities that acted early, like St. Louis, fared far better than Philadelphia, which held a crowded parade on 28 September 1918 and lost more than a thousand people in ten days.

Further waves followed into 1919 and 1920. In the United States average life expectancy fell by about twelve years in 1918 alone. The pandemic overwhelmed hospitals and undertakers, left countless orphans and widows, and disrupted economies already strained by the war.

Q130796.title: Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact
paras: The Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact was the non-aggression treaty between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union signed in Moscow in the early hours of 24 August 1939 and dated 23 August, by the Soviet foreign minister Vyacheslav Molotov and the German foreign minister Joachim von Ribbentrop, in Stalin's presence. Each side promised not to attack the other or help any third party that did. A secret protocol divided Eastern Europe between them.

In March 1939 Hitler had broken the Munich agreement and occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia, and Poland looked to be next; Britain and France guaranteed Poland's independence on 31 March and courted the Soviet Union. Hitler, whose generals feared a two-front war, began sounding out Stalin instead, hinting that the Soviets could have part of Poland. On 20 August he asked Stalin to receive his foreign minister, and on 22 August Ribbentrop flew to Moscow. The pact came as a shock to the world, given the two regimes' open hostility; Hitler had called the Soviet Union the greatest danger to civilisation only two years before.

Under the secret protocol Germany and the Soviet Union agreed to partition Poland and assigned Latvia, Estonia, Finland and Bessarabia to the Soviet sphere; Lithuania was moved to the Soviet sphere in a further agreement in September. Freed of the threat from the east, Hitler invaded Poland on 1 September 1939; Britain and France declared war on 3 September, and on 17 September the Red Army invaded Poland from the east. In 1940 the Soviet Union took land from Finland after the Winter War and annexed Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Romania's Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina.

The pact lasted less than two years: on 22 June 1941 Germany invaded the Soviet Union. The existence of the secret protocol, proven in the West at the Nuremberg trials, was officially denied by the Soviet Union until December 1989, when a commission set up under Mikhail Gorbachev confirmed it and the Soviet government condemned it.

Q12546.title: The Crusades
Q12546.place: The eastern Mediterranean, from Anatolia to Egypt
paras: The Crusades were a series of military campaigns launched by the papacy between 1095 and 1291 against the Muslim rulers of the Holy Land, to win back and then defend Jerusalem and the holy places for Christendom. They began when Pope Urban II, answering an appeal from the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos for help against the Seljuk Turks, called on Western Christians at the Council of Clermont in November 1095 to take up arms, promising spiritual rewards to those who went.

The response was enormous. A popular 'People's Crusade' under the preacher Peter the Hermit set out first and was destroyed by the Turks in Anatolia, and some crusaders massacred Jews in the Rhineland towns in 1096. The main armies, under leaders such as Godfrey of Bouillon, Raymond of Saint-Gilles and Bohemond of Taranto, left in August 1096, took Nicaea in 1097 and Antioch in June 1098, and in July 1099 captured Jerusalem, slaughtering many of its inhabitants. They set up four crusader states, at Jerusalem, Edessa, Antioch and Tripoli, defended by castles and by new military orders such as the Templars and Hospitallers.

Muslim rulers struck back. Zangi of Mosul took Edessa in 1144; the Second Crusade that followed, led by Louis VII of France and Conrad III of Germany, failed before Damascus. Saladin, who united Egypt and Syria, destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem at Hattin in 1187 and took the city. The Third Crusade of Frederick Barbarossa, Philip II of France and Richard I of England regained much of the coast but not Jerusalem, and in 1192 Richard made peace with Saladin. The Fourth Crusade turned against Christian Constantinople, which it sacked in 1204.

Later crusades against Egypt failed, though the Emperor Frederick II regained Jerusalem by treaty for a decade in 1229. The Mamluks, who took power in Egypt and halted the Mongols in 1260, conquered the remaining crusader strongholds, ending with Acre in 1291. Crusading went on elsewhere, against Muslims in Spain, pagans around the Baltic and heretics in southern France, but faded with the Reformation. During the crusades the wealth of the Church and the authority of the popes grew.

Q254106.title: Crimean War
Q254106.place: Crimea, the Danube and the Black Sea
paras: The Crimean War, from October 1853 to February 1856, was fought between the Russian Empire and an alliance of the Ottoman Empire, France and Britain, joined in 1855 by the Kingdom of Sardinia. It is remembered for the Charge of the Light Brigade, for Florence Nightingale's nursing, and as one of the first wars fought with modern technology and reported in photographs.

It grew out of a quarrel between Catholic and Orthodox Christians over the holy places of Jerusalem and Bethlehem under Ottoman rule. Tsar Nicholas I demanded that the sultan recognise him as protector of all the Orthodox subjects of the Ottoman Empire, and when the sultan refused, Russia occupied the Danubian principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia. The Ottomans declared war in October 1853. In November a Russian fleet destroyed an Ottoman squadron at Sinop on the Black Sea, killing nearly 2,000 Ottoman sailors, and the outcry, together with fear of Russian expansion towards the Mediterranean and India, brought Britain and France into the war in March 1854.

In September 1854 the allies landed in Crimea to take Sevastopol, the base of Russia's Black Sea fleet, and routed the Russians at the Alma. The expected short siege lasted eleven months. At Balaklava in October 1854 the 93rd Highlanders' 'thin red line' held off Russian cavalry, but a misunderstood order sent the Light Brigade charging into a valley ringed by Russian guns; of about 670 men, 110 were killed and 160 wounded. The Russians were beaten again at Inkerman in November, fought in thick fog. The armies suffered terribly through the winter of 1854-55 from cold, storms and diseases such as cholera, and the reports of the conditions prompted Nightingale's work in the military hospitals.

In September 1855 French troops stormed the Malakoff redoubt, and the Russians abandoned Sevastopol. Isolated and threatened by Austria, Russia sued for peace, and the Treaty of Paris of 30 March 1856 ended the war; Russia gave up its conquests and was forbidden to keep warships on the Black Sea. The war saw rifles made in factories, railways, the telegraph and explosive naval shells, and was among the first to be documented by war correspondents and photographers.

Q33143.title: Seven Years' War
Q33143.place: Europe, North America, India and the seas
paras: The Seven Years' War of 1756 to 1763 was a global conflict between the great powers of Europe, fought in Europe, in North America (where its American part is known as the French and Indian War), in India and on the oceans. On one side stood Britain and Prussia, on the other France, Austria and Russia, with Sweden, and from 1762 Spain.

Two rivalries drove it. In Europe, Austria wanted to recover the rich province of Silesia, which Frederick II ('the Great') of Prussia had seized in the War of the Austrian Succession of 1740 to 1748. To do so it broke with tradition and allied itself with its old enemy France, while Britain allied with Prussia, a reversal known as the Diplomatic Revolution. Overseas, Britain and France were competing for empire, above all in the Ohio valley in North America, where fighting had already begun in 1754, when a young George Washington clashed with French forces and was forced to surrender at Fort Necessity.

Frederick struck first, invading Saxony in August 1756. Facing far larger enemies, he won great victories at Rossbach and Leuthen in late 1757, but by 1760 Russian and Austrian troops briefly occupied Berlin, and Prussia was near exhaustion when the Russian empress Elizabeth died; her successor Peter III, an admirer of Frederick, made peace in 1762, the 'Miracle of the House of Brandenburg'. Britain, under William Pitt, paid subsidies to Prussia and threw its own strength into the war at sea and in the colonies: it took Louisbourg and Fort Duquesne in 1758, won Quebec in 1759 and Montreal in 1760, beat the French navy at Lagos and Quiberon Bay in 1759, and took French posts in the Caribbean, West Africa and India.

The Treaty of Paris of February 1763 gave Britain Canada and Spanish Florida, while France lost its possessions in North America and Britain established its commercial dominance in India. The Treaty of Hubertusburg, signed days later, left Silesia with Prussia, confirming it as a great power. Britain emerged as the leading colonial and naval power, but deep in debt; its efforts to make the American colonies pay a share led to the American Revolution, in which France took its revenge.

Q49100.title: Yom Kippur War
paras: The Yom Kippur War, the fourth major Arab-Israeli war, began on 6 October 1973, when Egypt and Syria launched a surprise attack on Israel on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, when many Israeli soldiers were away observing the holy day. Most of the fighting took place in the Sinai Peninsula and on the Golan Heights, which Israel had occupied since 1967.

Egypt's president Anwar Sadat, who had taken office in 1970, wanted to recover Sinai and to force a peace on better terms than Israel would then offer; his peace proposals, the last in February 1973, had been rejected by Golda Meir's government. In 1972 he expelled some 20,000 Soviet advisers, opened channels to Washington and planned a joint attack with Syria.

Armed with modern Soviet weapons, Egyptian forces crossed the Suez Canal in Operation Badr and dug in on the eastern bank, while Syrian forces advanced on the Golan. Iraqi troops joined the war and Jordan helped Syria. Once fully mobilised, Israel threw back the Syrians and, after a failed Egyptian advance into Sinai on 14 October, crossed the canal itself, driving north and south to cut off the Egyptian Second and Third Armies. A large American airlift of arms helped Israel. A UN ceasefire on 22 October broke down the next day, and a second, on 25 October, ended the fighting.

Israel won on the battlefield but at heavy cost, and anger at the lack of preparation led Golda Meir to resign in April 1974. Egypt's early successes restored Sadat's prestige and let him negotiate: disengagement agreements in 1974 returned part of Sinai, the Camp David Accords of 1978 and the peace treaty of 1979 made Egypt the first Arab state to recognise Israel, and the last of Sinai was handed back in 1982.

Q82664.title: Iran–Iraq War
Q82664.place: The Iran–Iraq border, Khuzestan and the Persian Gulf
paras: The Iran–Iraq War began on 22 September 1980, when Iraq under Saddam Hussein invaded Iran, and lasted almost eight years, until a United Nations ceasefire in August 1988. With around half a million dead, it was one of the deadliest conventional wars of the 20th century, and it ended with neither side gaining anything.

The two states had long quarrelled over the Shatt al-Arab, the waterway that forms their southern border and is Iraq's only outlet to the Gulf; in the Algiers Agreement of 1975 Iraq had given up part of its control in return for Iran ending its support for Kurdish rebels in Iraq. The Iranian Revolution of 1978-79 changed everything: Saddam, who became president in July 1979, feared that Ayatollah Khomeini's Shia revolution would spread to Iraq's Shia majority, and saw a chance to strike while Iran's army was weakened by the upheaval.

Iraqi aircraft struck Iranian air bases and its army invaded the oil-rich province of Khuzestan, taking the port of Khorramshahr after a long battle. But Iranian resistance, reinforced by revolutionary militias, stiffened, and by 1982 Iran had won back almost all the lost ground. Khomeini refused peace and carried the war into Iraq, launching repeated offensives towards Basra with massed 'human wave' attacks. The front settled into a stalemate of trench warfare; both sides attacked cities and oil installations, and Western navies came into the Gulf to protect shipping. Iraq, backed by Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and other Arab states and tacitly by Western powers, used chemical weapons against Iranian troops and Kurdish civilians.

In 1988 Iraqi offensives convinced Iran's leaders they could not win, and Iran accepted Security Council Resolution 598; the war formally ended on 20 August 1988. Estimates of total casualties run from 1 to 2 million. Iraq came out with a strengthened army and more power in the region, and two years later Saddam invaded Kuwait.

Q128160.title: Cuban Missile Crisis
paras: The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 was a thirteen-day confrontation between the United States and the Soviet Union over Soviet nuclear missiles secretly being installed in Cuba, and is often seen as the moment the Cold War came closest to nuclear war.

Cuba, under Fidel Castro since 1959, had aligned itself with the Soviet Union, and the United States had backed the failed Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961. The Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev sent missiles to Cuba to deter another invasion and to offset American nuclear superiority, including the Jupiter missiles the United States had placed in Italy and Turkey. On 14 October 1962 an American U-2 spy plane photographed a medium-range missile site being built, about 90 miles from Florida.

President John F. Kennedy was briefed on 16 October and met with a group of advisers, the ExComm. Rejecting air strikes and an invasion for the moment, he chose a naval 'quarantine' of Cuba, announced in a television address on 22 October, and demanded that the missiles be removed. On 24 October Soviet ships heading for Cuba stopped short of the blockade line. Tension peaked on 'Black Saturday', 27 October: a U-2 was shot down over Cuba, killing its pilot, Major Rudolf Anderson, and U.S. ships dropped signalling depth charges on the Soviet submarine B-59, unaware that it carried a nuclear torpedo.

Khrushchev had offered on 26 October to withdraw the missiles in return for an American promise not to invade Cuba, and on 27 October asked for the removal of the American missiles in Turkey too. Kennedy publicly accepted the first offer, while his brother Robert privately assured the Soviet ambassador that the missiles in Turkey would go. On 28 October Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles; the blockade ended on 20 November once missiles and bombers had left. A direct hotline between Washington and Moscow followed in 1963, and treaties limiting nuclear weapons, but the Soviets also expanded their arsenal of intercontinental missiles.

Q5086.title: Berlin Wall built
paras: In the early hours of 13 August 1961 the communist government of East Germany (the GDR) began sealing off West Berlin with barbed wire and concrete blocks. Within two weeks the first wall had gone up, and over the following years it became a guarded barrier with a 'death strip' that divided Berlin for 28 years, the best-known symbol of the Cold War.

After the Second World War Germany and Berlin were each divided into four occupation zones. West Berlin, held by the United States, Britain and France, lay deep inside Soviet-controlled East Germany, and the Soviet attempt to force the Western powers out with the blockade of 1948-49 had failed in the face of the Berlin Airlift. West Berlin then became the main escape route from the East: before the wall about 3.5 million East Germans, a fifth of the population and many of them doctors, engineers, teachers and skilled workers, left for the West. The flight speeded up in 1961; in July alone some 30,000 fled, and on 12 August about 2,400 crossed in a single day.

The GDR leader Walter Ulbricht had assured the press in June that no one intended to build a wall; the initiative appears to have come from the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev, who gave his approval at the start of August. Officially the 'Anti-Fascist Protection Rampart' was to keep out Western 'fascists'; its real purpose was to stop people leaving. Families and neighbourhoods were split and the free movement of Berliners to work and shops across the city ended. In October 1961 American and Soviet tanks faced each other at Checkpoint Charlie. Kennedy, who accepted the wall as 'a hell of a lot better than a war', told West Berliners in 1963, 'I am a Berliner.'

More than 5,000 people escaped across the wall, but between 136 and more than 200 were killed by the East German authorities while trying. The wall stood until 9 November 1989, when, after weeks of protests, the GDR announced that its citizens could cross freely and crowds poured through the checkpoints. Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990.

Q52418.title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
paras: On the morning of Sunday 7 December 1941 the Imperial Japanese Navy made a surprise air attack on the U.S. Pacific Fleet at its base at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. Launched from six aircraft carriers under Admiral Chūichi Nagumo, 353 Japanese aircraft struck in two waves beginning at 7:48 a.m. All eight American battleships present were damaged and four were sunk, nearly 20 ships and more than 300 aircraft were damaged or destroyed, 2,403 Americans were killed and 1,178 wounded. Japan lost 29 aircraft and five midget submarines.

Japan, at war with China since 1937, had met with mounting American sanctions and trade embargoes, including on oil, and months of talks had led nowhere. Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto planned the strike to knock out the Pacific Fleet so that it could not interfere with Japan's planned conquests in Southeast Asia, hoping for rapid gains and a negotiated peace. The American command expected any attack to fall on the European colonies to the south, not on Hawaii, some 4,000 miles from Japan, and the fleet lay crowded around Ford Island.

At 8:10 a bomb penetrated the forward magazine of the battleship USS Arizona, which blew up and sank with more than 1,000 men; about half of all the dead were aboard her. Torpedoes capsized the USS Oklahoma. Within less than two hours the attack was over. Within the same seven hours Japan also attacked the Philippines, Guam and Wake Island and the British in Malaya, Singapore and Hong Kong.

Japan had failed to cripple the fleet: its three carriers were at sea, and the base's oil storage and repair yards were left untouched; most of the damaged battleships were later repaired. On 8 December President Franklin D. Roosevelt called 7 December 'a date which will live in infamy', and Congress declared war on Japan with a single vote against; Britain declared war the same day. On 11 December Germany and Italy declared war on the United States, bringing it fully into the Second World War.

sources.title: Pearl Harbor: Facts, Date & Attack Summary

claims: Japan made a surprise attack on Pearl Harbor on Sunday 7 December 1941, just before 8 a.m.
The attack force under Nagumo launched at 7:48 a.m.; 353 aircraft in two waves from six carriers.
All eight battleships were damaged and four sunk; nearly 20 ships and over 300 aircraft damaged or destroyed; 2,403 Americans killed and 1,178 wounded.
Japanese losses: 29 aircraft and five midget submarines; 64 killed per Wikipedia (55 airmen, 9 submariners), 129 per HISTORY.com.

Japan's war on China from 1937; US sanctions and embargoes including oil; failed negotiations; Yamamoto planned a pre-emptive strike to keep the fleet from interfering in Southeast Asia, hoping for a negotiated peace.
US intelligence expected attacks on European colonies to the south; Hawaii is about 4,000 miles from Japan; the fleet was moored around Ford Island.
At 8:10 a bomb hit Arizona's forward magazine; it sank with more than 1,000 men; half the dead were on Arizona; Oklahoma capsized; the attack lasted less than two hours.
Over seven hours Japan also attacked the Philippines, Guam, Wake, Malaya, Singapore and Hong Kong.
The three US carriers were at sea; oil storage and repair facilities were not attacked.
Most damaged battleships were repaired (all but Arizona and Utah per HISTORY.com); Roosevelt's 'infamy' speech on 8 December.
Congress declared war with one vote against (Jeannette Rankin).
The UK and US declared war on Japan on 8 December; on 11 December Germany and Italy declared war on the US.

HISTORY.com says six ships were sunk or destroyed and lists the target ship USS Utah among the battleships; Wikipedia says four of the eight battleships present were sunk. American deaths agree at 2,403.
